title: greedy choices, invariants, and correctness proofs
concepts: A greedy algorithm makes an irrevocable locally chosen step and relies on a proof that the choice can still lead to a globally optimal solution.
A plausible local rule is only a hypothesis; small counterexamples, exhaustive search on tiny inputs, or comparison against a brute-force oracle can expose false greedy claims.
An exchange argument transforms an optimal solution to include the greedy choice without making it worse, establishing that some optimum agrees with the algorithm.
A staying-ahead proof compares the greedy partial solution with any competing solution after each step using a suitable invariant.
A greedy-choice property and optimal substructure often appear together, but neither should be assumed from a few examples; the proof must match the actual problem constraints.
Sorting by an endpoint, ratio, deadline, or value can expose a useful decision order, but the objective and feasible-set structure determine which ordering is valid.
Greedy fails when early choices consume resources needed for a better later solution; dynamic programming may be required when different partial choices need comparison.
Proof and complexity are separate: a fast algorithm still needs a correctness argument, while sorting or a heap may dominate the runtime of a greedy scan.
